files.why: Add a zod DTO schema for the per-customer feature-flag server response (snake_case), kept inside data/ per the DTO rule.
Add fetchRescheduleEnabled(customerId) that hits the flags endpoint and parses the DTO, so the toggle is read at runtime rather than at build time.
Add an MSW handler serving a per-customer reschedule flag so the flow can be flipped on/off in dev/demo without redeploying, matching how every other endpoint is mocked.
Thread a rescheduleEnabled flag into canReschedule/validateReschedule so the domain rule itself enforces the toggle (pure, framework-free) instead of relying on UI hiding alone.
Fetch and expose rescheduleEnabled for the current customer so the view knows whether to show the reschedule entry points.
Honor the flag when submitting so an in-flight form still refuses when reschedule is disabled, matching the new policy signature.
Hide/disable the 'Reschedule' button and inline RescheduleForm when the flag is off — the actual user-facing on/off switch.

uncertain: Home for the flag source. Feature flags are cross-cutting infra, but the constitution says everything lives in a slice or shared/, shared/ forbids domain nouns AND endpoints (transport-only), and 'reschedule' is a domain noun. So I placed the fetch inside scheduling/data. If billing (or others) soon need runtime flags too, this becomes duplicated and may justify a dedicated 'platform'/'flags' slice or a generic shared/lib flag-evaluation primitive fed by an app-level fetch — but rule 7 says duplicate until the 3rd same-reason use, so scheduling-local is correct today.

Whether to add scheduling/data/store.ts to cache the flag (billing has data/store.ts, so it is structurally legal) versus fetching inline in the composable. The README's 'Pinia — one store, on purpose' ethos argues against introducing a second store, so I lean toward no store.
Whether data/mappers.ts needs touching. If the flag response is a trivial boolean it needs no core mapping; if it carries structure it should map DTO->core like appointments do.

Whether the gate belongs in core/policy.ts at all versus being a pure UI concern. I put it in policy because canReschedule already encodes reschedule availability and the server should be authoritative, but a reviewer might prefer keeping core untouched and gating only in ui/.
questions: How is the 'current customer' identified? There is no auth/session/tenant infra; clientId is hardcoded to 'c-ana' in ClientOverviewView. The per-customer flag needs a real source for the active customer id.
Is 'customer' the same entity as the domain's 'client', or an account/tenant that owns multiple clients? This determines the key the flag is evaluated on.

Is this UI-only UX gating, or must the backend also reject reschedule PATCH requests for disabled customers? MSW only mocks it; UI hiding is bypassable, so I assumed server-authoritative but need confirmation.

Where does the flag come from in production — an existing flag service (LaunchDarkly/etc.), a config endpoint, or a brand-new backend endpoint whose contract we must define? MSW is only the mock stand-in.
Freshness/refetch expectations: must flipping the flag off mid-session immediately close an already-open reschedule form, and is any caching/TTL acceptable, or must it be fetched fresh on each visit?
